title: Ki Tavo: a wandering Aramean (Deuteronomy 26:5)
hookLine: "A wandering Aramean was my father", now at the heart of the Passover Haggadah

cards: At the Passover seder, the Haggadah reaches the telling of the Exodus itself, a long stretch of verses and commentary. Look closely at the verses it's built on, and they aren't from the book of Exodus.
They're from Deuteronomy, from the speech of the farmer with his basket. The Haggadah reads his few lines slowly, phrase by phrase, as the backbone of the night's story.
And it starts with a phrase readers still argue over.

teach.b: In the old Jewish translation, the speech begins: "A wandering Aramean was my father, and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there, few in number; and he became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous."
In Hebrew, arami oved avi. Three words, and readers don't agree on what they say.
Oved can mean wandering, lost, or perishing. Commentators like Ibn Ezra and Rashbam read it plainly: my ancestor, Jacob, or perhaps Abraham, was a wandering Aramean, a man without land of his own.
The Haggadah, and Rashi after it, read it another way: an Aramean, Laban, tried to destroy my father Jacob.
Two readings, both kept. One says, we came from wanderers. The other says, we came through danger.
Now notice what the farmer is doing. Standing with his own harvest, settled at last, the first thing out of his mouth is: we were not always settled. My people were strangers once.
And he says my father, not their father. It's personal.
The Mishnah asks the same of everyone at the seder: begin with the shame and end with the praise, and tell it as your own story.

The Torah ties that memory to its law: love the stranger, it says elsewhere, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt. One line of family history, and a rule for how to treat the newcomer next door.

how: Deuteronomy 26:5–8 is the core text of the Maggid section of the Passover Haggadah, where it is read and expounded phrase by phrase, opening with the Haggadah's reading of 'arami oved avi'.

games.q: inside three words — tap the pairs.

s: the verses the seder's telling is built on come from the book of Exodus
they come from Deuteronomy 26, the farmer's speech.
Rashi and the Haggadah read the Aramean as Laban
an Aramean sought to destroy my father.

wandering, lost, perishing: the readings differ.

games.q: you're the farmer, settled, your harvest in a basket at the altar. what's the first thing the Torah has you say?
o: a story: my father was a wandering Aramean.
a request for next year's rain.
games.why: before any thanks for the harvest, he tells where his people came from: wanderers, then slaves, then rescued.

practice: Go back as far as you know in your family: a grandparent, a name on an old document, or just a guess, and what they carried or left behind.
Try to say it in one sentence, the way the farmer does, something like: my grandmother crossed an ocean with one suitcase.
If you don't know your family's story, that not-knowing is part of many families' story too; hold whatever line you have, and let it sit.
